headings.title: Introduction to Artificial Respiration and Basic Concepts
headings.content: Artificial respiration encompasses all procedures and techniques utilized to assist or replace spontaneous pulmonary ventilation when a patient's respiratory system fails to maintain adequate gas exchange. In emergency nursing practice in Nigeria, understanding these foundational concepts is vital for saving lives in acute care settings, accident and emergency units, and community health outreaches. Normal respiration relies on an intact central nervous system, patent airways, functional chest wall mechanics, and adequate alveolar-capillary membrane diffusion. When any of these components fail, hypoxia and hypercapnia rapidly develop, leading to cellular anoxia, multi-organ dysfunction, and cardiac arrest if uncorrected. Artificial respiration can be delivered via non-invasive methods such as mouth-to-mouth or bag-valve-mask ventilation, or via invasive mechanical ventilation. Nursing students must recognize that prompt intervention restores oxygen delivery to vital organs, particularly the brain and myocardium. Basic airway clearance, positioning, and immediate manual rescue breathing form the cornerstone of basic and advanced life support protocols taught across Nigerian nursing institutions. Recognizing early signs of respiratory failure—such as tachypnea, use of accessory muscles, cyanosis, and altered mental status—allows nurses to initiate artificial support before complete respiratory arrest occurs. Mastery of these concepts ensures that student nurses transition smoothly into competent clinical practitioners capable of acting decisively during critical emergencies.

headings.title: Indications and Clinical Assessment for Respiratory Support
headings.content: Clinical assessment for respiratory support requires a systematic nursing approach utilizing the airway, breathing, and circulation (ABC) framework. Nurses must be adept at identifying precise indications for artificial respiration, which include acute respiratory failure, severe head injury with altered Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS), cardiac arrest, neuromuscular diseases affecting respiratory muscles, and severe drug overdoses. Assessment involves observing chest wall expansion, auscultating breath sounds bilaterally, measuring respiratory rate and depth, and monitoring arterial blood gases (ABGs) or pulse oximetry. In many Nigerian healthcare facilities where continuous ABG analysis may be limited, clinical observation of central cyanosis, paradoxical chest movements, exhaustion, and a falling oxygen saturation (< 90%) serve as critical triggers for intervention. Furthermore, a patient with a GCS score of 8 or less typically cannot protect their own airway and requires immediate advanced airway support. Nurses must document baseline respiratory parameters and continuously re-evaluate the patient's response to any initiated oxygen therapy or manual ventilation. Prompt and accurate clinical assessment prevents delayed interventions, reduces patient morbidity, and ensures that limited emergency resources are allocated efficiently to patients who require immediate ventilatory assistance.

headings.title: Manual Ventilation Techniques and Equipment
headings.content: Manual ventilation is an essential skill for nurses providing temporary or emergency respiratory support. The most common tool used in clinical practice is the bag-valve-mask (BVM) device, often referred to by brand names like Ambu bag. A standard BVM consists of a self-inflating bag, a non-rebreathing valve, an oxygen reservoir, and a transparent facemask. To achieve effective manual ventilation, the nurse must ensure an airtight seal using the 'E-C clamp' technique: the thumb and index finger form a 'C' shape to press the mask down, while the remaining three fingers form an 'E' shape along the lower jaw to lift it into the mask. Proper head-tilt, chin-lift or jaw-thrust maneuvers must be performed first to open the airway, unless a cervical spine injury is suspected, in which case jaw-thrust alone is used. Nurses must deliver breaths smoothly over one second, observing for visible chest rise, and avoiding excessive volume or rapid rates that can lead to gastric insufflation, regurgitation, and aspiration. Supplementing the BVM with high-flow oxygen (10–15 liters per minute) connected to the reservoir significantly increases the fraction of inspired oxygen delivered to the patient. Regular inspection and cleaning or replacement of BVM components are mandatory nursing responsibilities to maintain emergency readiness in hospital wards and clinics across Nigeria.

headings.title: Advanced Airway Management in Emergency Settings
headings.content: Advanced airway management involves securing the airway with devices that isolate the trachea, protect against aspiration, and facilitate mechanical ventilation. These devices include endotracheal tubes (ETTs), supraglottic airway devices like laryngeal mask airways (LMAs), and surgical airways such as cricothyroidotomy or tracheostomy. Endotracheal intubation is the gold standard for definitive airway management during prolonged resuscitation or surgery. Nursing students must assist the physician or advanced practice nurse during intubation by gathering equipment (suction, laryngoscope with working light blades, ETTs of appropriate sizes, stylet, syringe, and bag-valve-mask), pre-oxygenating the patient, and monitoring vital signs. Following intubation, immediate verification of correct tube placement is critical; nurses must auscultate bilateral breath sounds (noting equal entry), listen over the epigastrium to rule out esophageal intubation, observe symmetrical chest expansion, and check for condensation in the tube. Securement of the ETT using tape or commercial holders prevents accidental extubation. In emergency scenarios where oral intubation fails, emergency surgical access like cricothyroidotomy may be performed. Post-intubation chest radiography is the definitive diagnostic method to confirm that the ETT tip is positioned approximately 3 to 5 centimeters above the carina, ensuring proper ventilation of both lungs.

headings.title: Mechanical Ventilation Principles and Nursing Care
headings.content: Mechanical ventilation is utilized when patients cannot maintain adequate ventilation or oxygenation independently. Ventilators deliver preset volumes or pressures of oxygen-enriched air based on settings configured by the medical team. Common modes include Synchronized Intermittent Mandatory Ventilation (SIMV), Assist-Control (AC) ventilation, and Continuous Positive Airway Pressure (CPAP). Nursing care for mechanically ventilated patients is comprehensive and demanding. Nurses must perform regular respiratory assessments, including monitoring ventilator alarms (high pressure, low pressure, apnea), checking settings against doctor orders, and ensuring humidification systems function properly to prevent mucous plugging. Oral care using chlorhexidine mouthwash must be performed every 2 to 4 hours to minimize the risk of Ventilator-Associated Pneumonia (VAP). Elevating the head of the bed to 30 to 45 degrees is a vital non-pharmacological intervention that prevents aspiration and VAP. Nurses also manage sedation and analgesia protocols, ensuring patients are comfortable yet safely responsive during assessment. Endotracheal suctioning is performed using sterile technique only when clinically indicated by adventitious breath sounds, coughing, or saw-tooth patterns on the ventilator flow waveform, rather than on a routine schedule. Frequent turning, skin care, and passive range of motion exercises prevent complications of immobility.

headings.title: Monitoring, Complications, and Troubleshooting
headings.content: Continuous monitoring and swift troubleshooting are paramount for patients receiving artificial respiration. Nurses must monitor vital signs, pulse oximetry, end-tidal carbon dioxide (ETCO2 / capnography), and ventilator parameters continuously. Ventilator alarms are critical safety features that must never be silenced or ignored; nurses must investigate every alarm immediately using the 'DOPE' mnemonic: D for Displacement of the tube, O for Obstruction (e.g., mucus plug, biting the tube), P for Pneumothorax, and E for Equipment failure. If the cause of distress cannot be immediately identified or fixed, the nurse must disconnect the patient from the mechanical ventilator and manually ventilate them with a BVM using 100% oxygen to determine if the issue is patient-related or machine-related. Common complications of artificial respiration include barotrauma (leading to pneumothorax), volutrauma, oxygen toxicity, hypotension due to increased intrathoracic pressure reducing venous return, and tracheal stenosis from prolonged intubation or excessive cuff pressure. Nurses monitor cuff pressures regularly, keeping them between 20 to 30 cmH2O to prevent tracheal ischemia while ensuring a proper seal. Prompt recognition of these complications allows for timely medical interventions, safeguarding patient recovery and preventing further physiological deterioration.

headings.title: Weaning and Post-Resuscitation Nursing Responsibilities
headings.content: Weaning from artificial respiration is the systematic process of transitioning a patient from mechanical ventilator support back to spontaneous breathing. Nursing responsibilities during weaning require close collaboration with the interdisciplinary healthcare team. Before weaning begins, the patient must meet specific clinical criteria: hemodynamic stability, adequate oxygenation (e.g., PaO2/FiO2 ratio > 200), resolution or improvement of the underlying acute illness, active cough and gag reflexes, and the ability to breathe spontaneously during a spontaneous breathing trial (SBT). During the SBT, nurses monitor the patient meticulously for signs of weaning failure, which include tachypnea, tachycardia, hypertension, diaphoresis, dyspnea, falling oxygen saturation, and cardiac arrhythmias. If failure occurs, the trial is stopped, ventilatory support is resumed, and the patient is allowed to rest. Once weaning is successful, extubation is performed. Post-extubation nursing responsibilities include monitoring for airway edema, stridor, hoarseness, and respiratory distress. Providing humidified oxygen via facemask or nasal cannula, encouraging deep breathing and coughing exercises, and performing frequent oral care support the patient through recovery. Nurses also provide emotional support and reassurance, as the weaning process can induce anxiety and fear in patients recovering from critical illness.
